questions.stem: The board conceded that its earlier expansion plans had been {1} — four new plants built on borrowed money in a single year — and resolved to {2}, shuttering two of them and freezing all hiring.
questions.explanation: "Conceded" marks the earlier plans as a fault, and building four plants on borrowed money is wasteful spending, so profligate is required; parsimonious and canny would both be self-congratulatory rather than confessional. The second blank is the corrective response — closing plants and freezing hiring is a sharp contraction, which is retrench; squander would repeat the error and speculate names risk-taking, not cutting back.

questions.stem: When the endowment lost a fifth of its value in a single year, the college had little choice but to {1}: sabbaticals were suspended, three departments were merged, and the new library was shelved indefinitely.
questions.explanation: The colon introduces a list of concrete cuts, so the blank must mean to reduce spending and operations under financial pressure: retrench and economize both do. Temporize (play for time) and improvise fit the grammar and the crisis tone but describe delay or ad-hoc coping rather than contraction, and speculate would mean gambling the remaining endowment — the opposite response.

questions.stem: Critics who had dismissed the director's earlier films as {1} — three-hour cuts from which no editor was permitted to remove a frame — were startled by the new work's {2} economy of means.
questions.explanation: A film whose maker refuses all editing is pleasing himself rather than his audience, which is precisely self-indulgent; ascetic and austere describe the restraint that is absent here and would contradict the dash clause. The second blank must praise the reversal — a stripped-down economy of means is spartan, whereas decadent and libertine would restate the old fault the sentence says was startlingly abandoned.

questions.stem: The first hundred pages of the memoir catalogue every meal the author ate in Rome; readers who had been promised a history of the papacy found the digression {1}.
questions.explanation: A writer devoting a hundred pages to his own dinners while the promised subject waits is gratifying himself at the reader's expense — the core sense of self-indulgent. Ascetic describes the abstemiousness the passage conspicuously lacks, and perspicacious, tentative and decorous all name qualities the disappointed readers are not complaining about.

questions.stem: Because the diary breaks off in 1847, biographers can only {1} about why Alcott left Boston so abruptly; the popular story that she was fleeing a creditor remains {2}, resting on gossip recorded thirty years after the fact.
questions.explanation: The missing diary removes the evidence, so the biographers can reason but not prove — they speculate; corroborate and substantiate both require the documentation the sentence says is gone. The second blank must match that evidentiary vacuum: a story resting on late gossip is conjectural, while incontrovertible and axiomatic would claim exactly the certainty the clause denies.

questions.stem: Rather than examining the underlying businesses and holding for years, Hudson {1} in railway shares, buying on rumor and selling within the week.
questions.explanation: Buying on rumor and flipping within a week is betting on price movement, the financial sense of speculate. Invested is the trap the sentence explicitly rules out — "rather than examining the underlying businesses and holding for years" describes the investor Hudson is not; retrenched and abstained describe pulling back, and extrapolated names a form of inference, not a trade.

questions.stem: The new curator's neon installations were conceived as a rebuke to the museum's {1} reputation: decades of brown galleries, hushed docents, and portraits acquired by committee.
questions.explanation: The colon supplies the content of the reputation — respectable, conventional and slightly lifeless — which staid and sedate both convey, and the word must be unflattering enough to warrant a rebuke. Venerable fits the old-institution tone but admires rather than deflates, iconoclastic is the curator's quality rather than the museum's, and phlegmatic describes an unexcitable temperament rather than institutional dullness.

questions.stem: The partners cultivated a determinedly {1} exterior — grey suits, surnames only, a lobby as hushed as a chapel — precisely because the trade that paid for it, buying distressed debt on the chance of a rebound, was too {2} to advertise.
questions.explanation: Grey suits, surnames and a chapel-like hush describe sober conventionality carried to the point of dullness, which is staid; facetious and iconoclastic would clash with every detail in the dash clause. The second blank must name what the sober façade conceals — buying distressed debt on the chance of a rebound is speculative, whereas decorous and somnolent would make the trade indistinguishable from the exterior and destroy the sentence's contrast.
